source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: Older GPT-3 models fall for intuitive traps (CRT, semantic illusions) more than humans do. ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mostly avoid them.
numbers: CRT: davinci-003 correct 5%, intuitive 80%; humans correct 38%, intuitive 55%; ChatGPT-3.5 correct 59%, intuitive 15%; GPT-4 correct 96%, intuitive 0%. Semantic illusions: davinci-003 fell for 72% (18% correct); ChatGPT-3.5 74% correct, GPT-4 88% correct (humans 26%).
limits: Tasks are CRT and Moses-type illusions, not anchoring or framing directly. Possible training contamination.
agent_relevance: Bias on traps depends strongly on model generation. Measure our own base model; do not assume human-like bias.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (chain-of-thought and few-shot arms)
finding: Chain-of-thought and worked examples cut intuitive errors for davinci-003. Blocking chain-of-thought left ChatGPT-3.5 almost unchanged and cost GPT-4 a little.
numbers: davinci-003 with CoT: correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29%. Few-shot: semantic illusions correct 18% to 54%, over 64% with 10+ examples; CRT type-1 accuracy 0% to about 78% after 30 examples. GPT-4 with CoT blocked: correct 95% to 88%, intuitive 0% to 10%.
limits: Examples of the same trap type teach that trap; gains may not transfer to new trap types.
agent_relevance: Worked examples of a specific trap help most. For S1 a short list of known input traps with examples may beat generic CoT.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (human comparison base)
finding: Their task difficulty was comparable to past human studies.
numbers: CRT correct 38% here vs 41% in the original study (n=3,428; chi2=3.60, p=.06). Semantic illusions: 64% intuitive here vs 52% in original (n=61).
limits: Human numbers come from earlier papers, not a matched sample.
agent_relevance: Model-vs-human bias comparisons are only rough.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and GPT-4o shift numeric estimates toward hints in the prompt. Stronger models are more consistently anchored. Hints labelled as from an expert anchor almost always.
numbers: Questions from an existing human anchoring dataset (up to about 62 items), hints H1 (control), H2 low and H3 high. All 12 questions with a 'PTF expert' hint showed an effect in every model. Time-period questions were 7 of 42 but 6 of 11 non-significant cases. Irrelevant first hint: no consistent effect.
limits: Small question set, forecasting items, no human arm run by the authors. Preliminary.
agent_relevance: Any number or expert opinion placed early in the context is a likely anchor. S1 should strip or defer such numbers.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in LLMs (mitigation arm)
finding: Chain-of-thought, 'principles of thought', 'ignore the anchor' and reflection did not remove anchoring in GPT-4 or GPT-4o. Showing both a low and a high hint pulled answers near the unbiased value when the hints bracketed it.
numbers: Mitigation t-tests still showed very small p-values for most questions. Both-anchor worked on 8 named questions (5,7,8,10,12,13,14,15) where hints straddled the benchmark, not on the rest.
limits: Needs well-chosen opposite hints. No pooled effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Supports a structural fix: gather hints from several directions before answering instead of telling the model to ignore one.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in LLMs (model strength note)
finding: Weaker GPT-3.5 gave more exceptions to anchoring, which authors attribute to noise rather than resistance.
numbers: Of 11 exceptions to anchoring, 9 came from GPT-3.5.
limits: Interpretation is the authors' guess.
agent_relevance: More capable does not mean less anchored.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Benchmark of 13,465 prompts on anchoring, framing, status quo, group attribution, primacy and more, in student-admission decisions. Framing effects appeared and differed by model.
numbers: GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under the 'reject' framing than the 'admit' framing (rates 0.375 admit vs 0.780 reject frame). Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Models: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Llama-2 7B and 13B. No clear status-quo bias.
limits: Admissions scenario only. GPT-4 shows framing in a direction that depends on the cell.
agent_relevance: Ready test set for S1 input rewriting and a template for measuring prompt-induced bias.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster) (mitigation arm)
finding: Self-help (the model rewrites its own prompt to remove bias) worked best overall. Few-shot contrastive and counterfactual examples often broke the model so it admitted or rejected nearly everything. Self-help needs a high-capacity model.
numbers: Self-help left biased prompt elements: GPT-4 group attribution 0%, framing 2.7%; Llama-2 13B framing 0%, Llama-2 7B 1.4%. GPT-3.5 reduced group-attribution prompts by only 8.9%. In the sequential anchoring task Llama models changed 40-52% of decisions when asked to debias afterwards.
limits: Mixed anchoring distances in Table 3; instruction failures flagged with asterisks.
agent_relevance: Supports an S1 step that rewrites input to strip framing words, run by a capable model and checked by code.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do Large Language Models Show Decision Heuristics Similar to Humans?
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and humans both showed anchoring, conjunction fallacy, availability pull, framing and endowment effects in simple prompts.
numbers: Anchoring: low anchor mean 20.83 (ChatGPT) vs 22.5 (humans); high anchor 105.97 vs 80.5; t(58)=8.78, p<.0001 for ChatGPT (30 trials per cell). ChatGPT-4, 5 trials per cell: 22.0 vs 94.33. Linda-type: ChatGPT chose the conjunction 18/20, humans 10/20. Phone availability: ChatGPT picked the anecdote-backed phone 20/20, humans 14/20. Framing: ChatGPT rated gain frame 5 vs loss frame 4 (1-7 scale) in 11/11 trials each; humans 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80)=3.86, p<.001.
limits: Tiny samples, jailbreak-style prompt ('agent that can do anything'), one wording per task.
agent_relevance: A self-generated random number still anchored the estimate, so S1 must not feed unrelated numbers.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases (framing)
finding: Codex and CodeGen copied an irrelevant framing line placed earlier in the prompt, and accuracy fell.
numbers: Original functional accuracy: Codex 32.9%, CodeGen 25.6%. With irrelevant preceding function plus framing line: Codex 2.4-4.9%, CodeGen 1.5-4.2%. Framing line output: Codex 91.7% vs 1.4% without (raise NotImplementedError); CodeGen 79.3% vs 0.0%.
limits: Code generation, greedy decoding, HumanEval, 2022 models.
agent_relevance: Stray text early in context gets copied. Keep prompts free of irrelevant earlier material.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases (anchoring and availability)
finding: Prepending a near-correct but buggy anchor function lowered accuracy and made outputs reuse parts of the anchor. Frequent training patterns also pulled outputs (availability analogue).
numbers: Anchor functions decreased functional accuracy; the anchor's loop and print lines appeared in generated solutions at rates that grew with the number of canonical lines in the anchor (Figure 4). Exact rates are in figures only.
limits: Exact rates not recoverable from the text layer. Availability here means frequent training examples, not ease of recall.
agent_relevance: Do not paste earlier failed attempts verbatim into the next attempt without a check; they act as anchors.

source: Malberg et al. (2025) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: 30 biases tested in 20 models with 30,000 generated tests. Framing and anchoring are among the strongest; availability is weak. Every model was biased on some.
numbers: Mean bias score (-1 to 1; random model about 0): Framing 0.41, Anchoring 0.39 (model range -0.05 to 0.67), Availability heuristic 0.11, all 30 biases average 0.13, mean absolute 0.36. Only Status-Quo and Disposition Effect were negative on average.
limits: Score is a control-vs-treatment contrast, not a human effect size. Tests generated with GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Make framing and anchoring the first two checks in S1; availability is less urgent.

source: Malberg et al. (2025) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs (baseline and failure rate)
finding: A random model scores about 0 on each bias, so positive scores mean systematic pull. The smallest Llama had low bias but often failed to decide.
numbers: Random: framing 0.01, anchoring 0.00, availability -0.05. Llama 1B failed to decide in 33% of tests.
limits: Low bias in weak models can mean low competence.
agent_relevance: When comparing scaffolds, report decision-failure rate next to bias score.

source: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models
finding: Seven models on classic tasks (Linda, Wason, Monty Hall and others). Most wrong answers were NOT the human bias; they were illogical or inconsistent.
numbers: GPT-4 correct with correct reasoning in 69.2% of responses, Claude 2 55.0%; Llama-2 7B incorrect in 77.5%.
limits: Seven 2023 models, small task set, tasks may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Do not assume LLM errors follow the human bias list. Check consistency by repeated sampling.

source: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi (2024) (inconsistency finding)
finding: Models gave different answers on repeats and sometimes reasoned correctly then stated a wrong final answer.
numbers: Bard explained the Wason task correctly but named the wrong card in its final answer; seen across all model families.
limits: Anecdotal examples plus aggregate counts.
agent_relevance: Extract the final answer by code from a fixed field and compare it with the reasoning.

source: Yax, Anllo, Palminteri (2024) Studying and improving reasoning in humans and machines
finding: New Linda/Bill vignettes (to avoid contamination) given to GPT-3 models and 128 humans. Models sit near chance; the Linda-vs-Bill gap grows with model sophistication. Humans beat models on Linda items but lose on the math version.
numbers: 1024 items (512 Linda, 512 Bill). Mean accuracy across models Bill 0.53, Linda 0.46 (chi2=78, p<.0001). Humans Bill 0.83, Linda 0.56. Joint-probability sums: humans 0.34 vs davinci-003 0.96. Large option-order effect in models, none in humans.
limits: GPT-3 family only.
agent_relevance: The conjunction gap is a representativeness pull, but option-order sensitivity is a separate error. Randomise option order in all choice checks.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 answered correctly or made human-like mistakes on 12 of 12 standard vignettes (including Linda) but made non-human mistakes on adversarial rewrites.
numbers: 12/12 standard vignettes correct or human-like; adversarial vignettes produced non-human errors (Figure 1).
limits: Few vignettes; davinci era.
agent_relevance: Textbook items are weak tests because of memorisation. Use rewritten variants.

source: Shaki, Kraus, Wooldridge (2023) Cognitive Effects in Large Language Models
finding: GPT-3 showed priming, distance, SNARC and size-congruity effects, but the abstract reports the anchoring effect as absent.
numbers: Anchoring test used small vs large anchors (large 71-90), 20 queries each; mean estimates differed by only a few points (e.g. 45.78 vs 42.04, 48.86 vs 46.31).
limits: Contradicts Suri and Lou. Different design: abstract anchors, base GPT-3, logit readout.
agent_relevance: Anchoring depends on how the anchor is presented; numeric hints framed as information anchor most.

source: Itzhak et al. (2024) Instructed to Bias: Instruction-Tuned Language Models Exhibit Emergent Cognitive Bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF raise decoy, certainty and belief biases compared with base models.
numbers: Bias scores (control vs treatment) are reported per model in Table 4; for example the certainty effect was 0.20 in DaVinci-003 and 0.15 in GPT-4 in one setting. Mistral, Flan-T5, GPT-3 and GPT-4 families tested.
limits: Biases are decoy, certainty and belief, adjacent to anchoring/framing. Table text alignment in the PDF is ambiguous.
agent_relevance: Alignment training may add human-like bias. Re-measure bias after any model swap.

source: Koo et al. (2024) Benchmarking Cognitive Biases in LLMs as Evaluators (COBBLER)
finding: 16 LLMs used as judges show order, bandwagon, salience and self-preference bias. A fake majority statistic sways them.
numbers: About 40% of comparisons showed strong bias overall. With '85% of people preferred System Star' over 70% of evaluations on average followed the bandwagon cue regardless of text quality. 11 of 15 models were drawn to first- or last-ordered output. Rank overlap with humans 44%.
limits: 50 instructions; includes non-Kahneman biases.
agent_relevance: Judge prompts must hide social cues, model names and order.

source: Koo et al. (2024) Benchmarking Cognitive Biases in LLMs as Evaluators (COBBLER) (self-preference)
finding: Largest models tend to prefer their own responses; real model names raise self-preference in smaller models.
numbers: Most large models preferred their own outputs in more than 50% of anonymised comparisons; with real names two smaller size groups showed increased self-preference (KOALA +100%).
limits: Indirect link to Kahneman biases.
agent_relevance: Do not let a model grade its own text; hide authorship.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing for Large Language Models in Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: Iterative loop: detect bias in the prompt, analyse it, rewrite the prompt, repeat until none is found. Lowest bias scores among tested methods for single and multiple injected biases (anchoring, bandwagon, loss aversion).
numbers: FOMC finance task, llama3.1-8b average bias score: vanilla 0.3805, CoT 0.3425, Reflexion 0.3830, multi-agent debate 0.5020, self-help 0.2100, SACD 0.1570. SACD averages 0.0300-0.1570 on FOMC, 0.0425-0.1790 on PubMedQA, 0.0400-0.1235 on LegalBench.
limits: Bias injected artificially. Several extra model calls per input.
agent_relevance: Direct template for an S1 loop: detect, analyse, rewrite input, with code deciding when to stop.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing for Large Language Models in Decision-Making (SACD) (what made it worse)
finding: Reflexion and multi-agent debate raised bias in some tasks because they feed back biased text. Few-shot was inconsistent.
numbers: FOMC gpt-3.5-turbo: debate average 0.5155. PubMedQA llama3.1-70b: Reflexion 0.5585. CoT average range 0.2470-0.6150 across domains.
limits: Single paper, own benchmark.
agent_relevance: Matches our guardrail on self-reflection: models reusing their own biased text amplify it.

source: Huang et al. (2026) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data (SynAnchors)
finding: Anchoring is common across 11 models and acts in early layers. Reasoning models are least anchored. Standard fixes fail.
numbers: Share of questions anchored 22% to 61%: Llama-3.1-8B 34.7%, Qwen2.5-7B 40.0%, GPT-4o 27.3%, DeepSeek-R1 25.0%, Qwen3-235B thinking 22.0%.
limits: Synthetic items; 'more or less than X' format.
agent_relevance: Real reasoning that revisits the anchor helps more than a warning; allow a thinking budget on estimates.

source: Huang et al. (2026) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data (SynAnchors) (mitigation arm)
finding: Prompt and decoding fixes barely moved anchoring; some made it worse.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B baseline 34.7%: question-aware prompt 36.8%, knowledge enhancement 50.5% (worse), self-improving 38.4%, adversarial finetuning 33.3%, DoLa 37.5-38.5%, Anti-DP 24.7%. Qwen2.5-7B baseline 40.0%: self-improving 48.0%.
limits: Two small open models.
agent_relevance: Adding more context (knowledge enhancement) can add anchors. Be careful with retrieval in S1.

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Bacchelli (2026) Mitigating Prompt-Induced Cognitive Biases in General-Purpose AI for Software Engineering
finding: On eight biases in software-engineering dilemmas, CoT and self-debiasing gave no significant per-bias gains. Eliciting best practices first and injecting them into the prompt cut bias sensitivity by 51% on average.
numbers: Median bias sensitivity: base 12.9%, CoT 16.1%, implication prompting 13.3%, impersonated self-debiasing 10.2%, bias warning 10.3%, both 8.3%. Sensitivity by bias type 5.9% (anchoring) to 35.3% (hindsight). New method: 51% average reduction, up to 73% (p<.001).
limits: Software dilemmas, cost-effective models; needs domain best practices.
agent_relevance: Add a step that states the task's own norms before answering; fits S1 restatement plus rule listing.
